title: What Suno’s October Studio update changes for hands-on creators
question: Do Suno’s new Studio controls help independent musicians turn their own ideas into work they would feel ready to release?
argument: Suno’s October 8 notes announce more precise clip placement, stretching, fade shaping, and floating windows. Those controls address editing tasks after an idea enters Studio. Recent musician accounts show distinct ways to bring ideas into Suno, but they do not test the October changes or establish that the resulting music is release ready.
synthesis: The cross-source inference is that finer timeline controls could matter to creators who start with recordings or generated material and then want to shape the result: Suno describes the controls, while Todd Edwards, Caleb Porzio, and Andrea Olsen describe different idea-to-output workflows. Their accounts cannot show whether the new controls work as announced, improve sound, or shorten production time.
limitations: The Studio changes are supported by Suno’s announcement, with no supplied independent test of those changes. The practitioner examples are individual accounts with different inputs and goals; Olsen also promotes a music course in her video. A creator who tested the October update on a release project is missing.

claims.statement: On October 8, Suno announced improved downbeat detection for new Studio clips and said it reduces manual alignment for non-rhythmic material such as a cappella vocals. This is a company claim, not a measured outcome.

locator.quote: We’ve made improvements to the detection of beat 1 in new clip creations. This means the timing of clips and takes on the Studio timeline is greatly improved, and there is more accuracy around the first downbeat in a clip. Now, the experience of working with non rhythmic clips, such as a cappella vocals, is smoother and the need to manually align is reduced.

claims.statement: Suno also announced shift-click-drag clip stretching, adjustable fade curves, and floating instrument and plug-in windows in Studio.

locator.quote: We’ve added a new feature where shift-click-dragging automatically timestretches a clip.
Now, you can shape the curve by dragging the node on the fade icon to create exponential- and logarithmic-shaped fades.
You can now pop out the wavetable synth, musical typing keyboard and expanded plug-in views to a floating window that can be dragged around the screen and even onto other monitors.

claims.statement: In MusicRadar’s interview, producer Todd Edwards said he put his own ideas into Suno-generated songs and cut the results into samples. His account describes his creative method, not a test of the October update or a verification of rights.

locator.quote: But I can put ideas in, make my own disco or soft rock songs, then take that out, cut them up and use them as samples

claims.statement: Podcaster Caleb Porzio described recording a rough guitar idea, adding a prompt, and listening to a Suno result he wanted to hear again. That is one listener-creator’s reaction to his own experiment.

In her video demonstration, Andrea Olsen uploaded her voice memo to Suno and judged the result to have followed her melody direction while still sounding like AI. She presents a single-song assessment, not evidence about the October Studio controls.

The newly announced editing controls could be useful after a creator brings a recording or generated sample into a project: Suno describes clip alignment and stretching, while Porzio describes starting with a rough recording and Edwards describes cutting generated material into samples. These sources do not establish that either creator used the new controls or that the controls improve a finished release.

locator.quote: We’ve added a new feature where shift-click-dragging automatically timestretches a clip.
But I can put ideas in, make my own disco or soft rock songs, then take that out, cut them up and use them as samples

title: What Suno quality tests actually measure
question: Which claims about Suno’s sound and creative control hold up when the tests use different songs, settings and outcomes?
argument: Current tests give creators useful checks, but no defensible overall v6 score. WaveDisco measured loudness and peaks across model versions; ytyng measured spectral differences across unmatched songs and export formats; a YouTube creator compared increasingly detailed directions for one song. Each test answers a narrower question than whether Suno will produce a release-ready track.
synthesis: WaveDisco’s same-prompt measurements and ytyng’s spectral analysis examine different audio properties, while On a Creative Journey judges vocal delivery after changing directions and later editing stems. Together they suggest that creators should test the property they care about—such as export loudness, tonal balance or response to direction—on their own material. The evidence cannot isolate a general model-quality effect: the samples are small, ytyng’s older tracks used different prompts and codecs, and the video creator says further iterations might explain the perceived improvement.
limitations: No blinded listening test or broad, matched set of creator-owned songs is supplied. Caleb Porzio’s podcast illustrates why an output can feel compelling to one listener while audible artifacts remain; his experience cannot establish how other creators or listeners would judge it. Perspectives from independent mastering engineers and release listeners are missing.

claims.statement: WaveDisco’s Serj regenerated three songs across v5.5 and three v6 variants with the same lyrics and prompt, then measured LUFS and True Peak. He found no consistent directional improvement on those measures.

locator.quote: Three songs, four model versions each, same lyrics and prompt every time. I measured LUFS and True Peak on every output with the same audio analysis pipeline, and compared WAV and MP3 formats where I had both.
On LUFS and True Peak, I didn't find one — the numbers move, but there's no consistent direction I can point to.

claims.statement: In the two WaveDisco songs with format comparisons, Serj reported a WAV–MP3 loudness gap for v5.5 and none for the three v6 variants. He explicitly cautioned that two songs are an illustration, not a study.

locator.quote: All three v6 models: LUFS difference is zero on both tracks.
To be clear: this is two songs where I had format comparisons. It's an illustration, not a study. Your tracks may behave differently.

claims.statement: Ytyng reported lower high-frequency energy in 24 v6 outputs than in 12 older tracks, but its comparison used different prompts and codecs. Its own limits leave open whether the difference came partly or wholly from the songs rather than the model.

locator.quote: v6 was down 2 to 3.4dB at 2 to 12kHz, and the spectral centroid was 36% lower.

The biggest one is that the songs and genres are not controlled. The v6 side is 2 songs and the pre-v6 side is 6 songs, each made from a different prompt. Spectral centroid moves a lot with genre, so I have not ruled out the possibility that part of this difference, or all of it, is "because the songs are different".
the v6 side is m4a (Opus 132kbps) and the pre-v6 side is mp3 (about 180kbps VBR), and I compare them as they are.

claims.statement: On a Creative Journey tested added performance directions on one song and judged a later version’s vocals smoother, but also acknowledged that repeated generations could explain the change. The creator subsequently cleaned stems and adjusted the vocal, so the final mix does not isolate prompting alone.

Produce Like a Boss’s Andrea Olsen supplied her own voice memo and lyrics, asked Suno to retain the melody, and reported that it largely followed her direction while still sounding artificial to her. This is a creator’s assessment of one input, not a general prompt-adherence rate.

On his podcast, Caleb Porzio said he wanted to listen to a song made from his rough recording, yet later described audible artifacts in other AI covers he had enjoyed. His account shows that enjoyment and artifact detection can coexist for one listener.

Taken together, these tests support checking separate properties on a creator’s own song rather than treating a loudness result, spectral result or preferred vocal take as an overall v6 quality verdict. This follows because the sources measure different outcomes under different controls; none establishes typical release readiness.

locator.quote: Measurements in this article were taken on three specific tracks using the same audio analysis pipeline on the same day. Suno's output characteristics vary across generations even with identical prompts — these numbers reflect one set of outputs, not a guaranteed behavior of any model version.
"How good a song is" has little to do with the spectrum, but this was about the only objective difference I could think of that a machine can measure, so I did it.

title: What to check before releasing a Suno-assisted song
question: What should a creator verify before release, and what evidence should they watch next?
argument: Keep a record of what you wrote, performed, uploaded and generated. Check the applicable Suno terms and the rules of each intended distributor or platform before release. Treat licensing promises, artist concerns and legal proceedings according to what each source actually establishes.
synthesis: A practitioner’s file-by-file record of human and generated contributions would help a creator explain their process. That practice matters alongside the Italian regulator’s investigation of Suno’s terms and musicians’ reported concerns about consent and compensation. Together, these sources support checking inputs and agreements before upload, but they do not establish the rights in any particular song or predict the investigation’s outcome. Deezer’s planned search filter adds a reason to watch platform classification after release; the supplied report does not show that the filter is live or how it would classify a particular Suno-assisted track.
limitations: The supplied material does not include the applicable primary Suno terms or a distributor rule for a specific release, so this brief cannot resolve rights or eligibility. The regulator has opened an investigation, not issued a finding. The podcast host offers a useful documentation method but also promotes his own music business. A distributor’s direct assessment of a documented Suno-assisted release is still missing.

claims.statement: Practitioner Josh of JG Beats Lab recommends keeping the dated original demo, lyrics, settings, retained stems, raw vocal takes and final master together, with each file’s origin recorded. This is his workflow advice, not a determination of ownership.

Dazed reports Zemi’s account that he makes beats and toplines, sings, uses Suno to change his voice, then mixes the result himself. His account shows why a creator may need to describe each contribution separately; the article does not independently verify every production step.

locator.quote: “Yes, the voice is AI, but all the rest is produced by me – the beats, the top lines, the production,” Zemi explains. “I sing the songs, bring it over into Suno to change the voice, and then mix it myself. The entire process behind it is human.”

claims.statement: The Italian Competition Authority has opened an investigation into whether Suno’s terms are unfair, including the scope of the license imposed on consumers. An opened investigation is not a finding against Suno.

locator.quote: The Italian Competition Authority has launched an investigation into Suno Inc., a US company that provides generative AI services specialising in music creation. The proceedings focus on Suno’s Terms of Service.
The scope of the license imposed on consumers as a condition for using the platform services seems to be insufficiently defined

claims.statement: The Los Angeles Times reports that musicians and songwriter groups question who can consent to licensing deals and who will be paid. It says the payout terms and opt-in numbers have not been disclosed, leaving the deals’ benefits to individual artists unverified.

locator.quote: But so far, none of them have disclosed what artists will be paid, how many artists have opted in, or how much input individual musicians have over whether their work is used.

Whether an artist opts out depends on who owns the rights. Songs typically carry two copyrights — one for the composition, usually held by songwriters and their publishers, and one for the sound recording, usually owned by the label.

claims.statement: Music Business Worldwide reports Suno’s statement that v6 training included licensed partner content and community interactions, including creations. It also reports that Sony and Universal’s new complaint makes allegations about training data; those allegations are contested claims, not court findings.

locator.quote: “v6 was trained on content licensed from our partners, interactions including creations and preference signals from our community, and the accumulated learnings from our team.

The filing alleges, on information and belief, that Suno trained v6 on synthetic audio files its users generated or altered with the earlier models, on preference data keyed to those outputs, or both.

claims.statement: Music Business Worldwide reports that Deezer plans a search toggle for fully AI-generated music before the end of 2026. A creator can watch its rollout and classification criteria, but this report does not show how the planned toggle would affect an AI-assisted song.

locator.quote: Deezer says it is introducing an on/off toggle that will let users exclude fully AI-generated music from their search results.
The French streaming service said on Tuesday (October 13) that the feature will roll out globally before the end of 2026.

claims.statement: Taken together, Josh’s documentation method, Zemi’s account of a mixed human and Suno workflow, and the regulator’s concern about license scope support recording what enters Suno and checking the applicable terms before uploading a release candidate. None of these sources determines the rights in a particular track.

locator.quote: “I sing the songs, bring it over into Suno to change the voice, and then mix it myself.
The scope of the license imposed on consumers as a condition for using the platform services seems to be insufficiently defined
